name: Veg Manchurian
cuisine: Indo-Chinese (Kolkata-born, now a Mumbai street-food and "Chinese corner" staple)

ingredients.name: Cabbage (patta gobi)
ingredients.householdMeasure: about ¾ cup very finely chopped or grated

ingredients.name: Carrot (gajar)
ingredients.householdMeasure: ¼ small carrot, finely grated (about 3 tbsp)

ingredients.name: Spring onion (hara pyaz), white and green parts
Sunflower or groundnut oil, for deep-frying
ingredients.householdMeasure: about 1 cup in the kadai; about 2 tsp absorbed

ingredients.name: Green chilli (hari mirch)
ingredients.householdMeasure: ½ small chilli, slit or chopped

ingredients.name: Onion (pyaz/kanda)
ingredients.householdMeasure: ¼ medium onion, cut into 1-cm squares (petals)

ingredients.name: Capsicum, green (Shimla mirch)
ingredients.householdMeasure: ¼ medium capsicum, cut into 1-cm squares

ingredients.name: Soy sauce (dark or all-purpose, e.g. Ching's)
Salt (namak)
ingredients.householdMeasure: a tiny pinch, only if needed after tasting

equipment: Chopping board and sharp knife, or a hand-operated chopper (pull chopper), for very fine cabbage
Small heavy kadai (about 18 cm), for deep-frying
Slotted spoon (jhara) and a plate lined with paper towel
Second pan, wok or kadai for the gravy (a wide non-stick pan works; high heat is useful but not essential)
Small cup and spoon for the cornflour slurry
Measuring spoons and a measuring cup (a normal teaspoon and a steel glass are fine stand-ins)

steps.title: Chop the cabbage
steps.text: Chop 50 g cabbage very finely (or grate it) into the mixing bowl.
steps.tip: Big pieces poke out and make the balls break in the oil; chop finer than you think.
steps.visualCue: Fine shreds, no pieces bigger than a grain of rice
steps.cameraCheck: The chopped cabbage in the bowl
steps.videoShot: A knife rocking through finely shredded cabbage.

steps.title: Grate the carrot
steps.text: Grate 20 g carrot (about ¼ small carrot) into the same bowl.
steps.visualCue: Fine orange shreds on top of the cabbage
steps.cameraCheck: Carrot and cabbage in the bowl
steps.videoShot: Carrot rubbed on the fine side of a grater.

steps.title: Chop the aromatics for the balls
steps.text: Finely chop 1 stalk spring onion (8 g), 1 small garlic clove (2 g), ½-inch ginger (2 g) and ½ green chilli (1 g). Add them to the bowl.
steps.visualCue: Small green and white flecks through the vegetables
steps.cameraCheck: The chopped aromatics on the board before adding
steps.videoShot: Knife chopping garlic and ginger together.

steps.title: Salt and rest the mix
steps.text: Add a pinch of salt (0.5 g) and a pinch of black pepper, mix with your hand and leave for 5 minutes.
steps.tip: Do not add water. The water the cabbage releases is enough to bind the flour (Hebbar's Kitchen, Sanjeev Kapoor).
steps.visualCue: The vegetables look wet and have shrunk a little; a few drops of water at the bottom of the bowl
steps.videoShot: A hand squeezing the mix, showing moisture.

steps.title: Add the flours
steps.text: Add 1½ tbsp maida (15 g) and 1 tbsp cornflour (8 g).
steps.visualCue: White flour heaped on top of the vegetables
steps.videoShot: Flour spooned into the bowl.

steps.title: Mix into a dough
steps.text: Mix and press with your fingers until all the flour is absorbed.
steps.tip: Too wet and sticky? Add 1 tsp more maida. Too dry and falling apart? Wait 2 minutes for more cabbage water, or add 1 tsp water.
steps.visualCue: A sticky, clumping mix that holds together when you squeeze a little in your fist; no dry flour left
steps.cameraCheck: A squeezed lump of mix holding its shape
steps.videoShot: A fist squeezing the mix, then opening to show a firm lump.

steps.title: Divide the mix
steps.text: Divide it into 6 equal portions (about 18 g each).
steps.visualCue: Six lumps of the same size
steps.videoShot: The mix pinched into six.

steps.title: Shape the balls
steps.text: Roll each portion between lightly oiled palms into a firm, round ball about 3 cm across.
steps.tip: Press firmly; loose balls open up in the oil.
steps.visualCue: Smooth, compact balls the size of a large walnut, with no loose shreds sticking out
steps.videoShot: Palms rolling a ball tight.

steps.title: Heat the frying oil
steps.text: Pour about 250 ml oil into the small kadai and heat on medium to about 170–180 °C.
steps.tip: Cool oil makes soggy, oily balls; smoking oil browns them outside while the inside stays raw.
steps.visualCue: A pea-sized bit of mix rises in 2–3 seconds with steady bubbles (not instantly with violent bubbling, which is too hot)
steps.cameraCheck: The oil test with the bit of mix
steps.videoShot: A tiny piece of mix rising and sizzling.

steps.title: Fry the balls
steps.text: Slide all 6 balls into the oil one by one. Do not touch them for the first 30 seconds, then turn them gently every minute on medium heat.
steps.tip: For extra-crisp restaurant-style balls, some cooks fry them pale first, rest 2 minutes, then fry again for 1 minute in hotter oil (Chef Sanjyot Keer's method).
steps.visualCue: Deep golden-brown all over, crisp shell, bubbles around them slowing down
steps.cameraCheck: The golden balls in the kadai
steps.videoShot: The slotted spoon rolling the balls in the oil.

steps.title: Drain the balls
steps.text: Lift them onto the paper-lined plate. Turn off the frying oil.
steps.tip: Let the leftover oil cool, strain it and reuse it once; do not reheat it many times.
steps.visualCue: Golden balls, paper showing light oil spots
steps.cameraCheck: The 6 fried balls on the paper
steps.videoShot: Balls lifted out, oil dripping back.

steps.title: Cut the gravy vegetables
steps.text: Cut ¼ onion (25 g) and ¼ capsicum (25 g) into 1-cm squares. Finely chop 2 small garlic cloves (4 g), ½-inch ginger (2 g) and 1 tsp spring onion whites (5 g); slit ½ green chilli.
steps.visualCue: Neat squares of onion and capsicum; a small heap of chopped garlic-ginger
steps.cameraCheck: The cut vegetables on the board
steps.videoShot: Capsicum cut into squares.

steps.title: Make the cornflour slurry
steps.text: Stir 2 tsp cornflour (6 g) into 2 tbsp (30 ml) water in a cup until smooth.
steps.visualCue: Milky-white liquid with no lumps
steps.videoShot: A spoon stirring the white slurry.

steps.title: Heat the gravy oil
steps.text: Heat 1 tsp (5 ml) oil in the second pan on high heat.
steps.visualCue: The oil shimmers and moves easily
steps.videoShot: Oil swirled in the pan.

steps.title: Fry the garlic, ginger and chilli
steps.text: Add the chopped garlic, ginger, green chilli and spring onion whites. Stir.
steps.tip: Garlic burns fast on high heat; have the onion ready.
steps.visualCue: Garlic just turning pale golden; strong garlic smell
steps.videoShot: Garlic sizzling and being tossed.

steps.title: Add the onion and capsicum
steps.text: Add the onion and capsicum squares and stir-fry on high heat.
steps.visualCue: Edges slightly translucent but still crunchy; capsicum bright green
steps.videoShot: Onion and capsicum tossed on high flame.

steps.title: Add the sauces
steps.text: Add 1 tsp soy sauce, 1 tsp red chilli sauce, 1½ tsp ketchup and a pinch of black pepper. Stir for 20 seconds.
steps.visualCue: Vegetables coated dark reddish-brown; sauces bubble at the edges
steps.videoShot: Soy sauce poured in a circle over the vegetables.

steps.title: Add the water
steps.text: Pour in 150 ml water and bring to a boil.
steps.visualCue: Thin brown liquid bubbling all over
steps.videoShot: Water poured into the pan, steam rising.

steps.title: Taste for salt
steps.text: Taste the liquid and add a tiny pinch of salt (0.3 g) only if needed.
steps.tip: Soy sauce is very salty; most cooks need no extra salt here.
steps.visualCue: Salty-tangy-spicy; it should taste slightly strong, since the balls are bland
steps.videoShot: A spoon lifted for tasting.

steps.title: Thicken the gravy
steps.text: Stir the slurry again and pour it in slowly while stirring. Simmer on medium.
steps.tip: Too thick? Add 2–3 tbsp water. Too thin? Simmer 1 more minute.
steps.visualCue: The gravy turns from cloudy to glossy and translucent and coats the back of the spoon
steps.videoShot: Slurry poured in a thin stream, gravy turning glossy.

steps.title: Add the vinegar
steps.text: Stir in ½ tsp vinegar and turn off the heat.
steps.visualCue: Sharp, tangy smell
steps.videoShot: Vinegar drizzled in.

steps.title: Add the balls
steps.text: Put the 6 fried balls into the gravy and turn them gently once to coat.
steps.tip: Add the balls only just before eating; they soak up gravy and turn soft within 10–15 minutes.
steps.visualCue: Balls glossy and half-covered in gravy
steps.videoShot: Balls dropped into the glossy gravy.

steps.title: Garnish and serve
steps.text: Transfer to a bowl and scatter 2 tsp spring onion greens on top.
steps.visualCue: Brown glossy gravy, golden balls, green garnish
steps.videoShot: Spring onion greens sprinkled over the steaming bowl.

reasons: the home bowl is mostly vegetables (about 130 g of cabbage, carrot, onion, capsicum and spring onion), low in saturated fat and cholesterol-free, with good vitamin C, K and A, and only about 13 g fat. But the balls are deep-fried and bound with refined maida and cornflour, protein is very low (about 4 g), and the sauces push sodium to about 850 mg (43% of the daily limit). Restaurant versions usually use more batter, reused frying oil, 1–2 tbsp soy sauce, MSG and sugar, and come with fried rice or noodles.

researchRating.basis: veg Manchurian is one of the most-searched and most-made Indo-Chinese dishes in India and a Mumbai street-food fixture (Tarla Dalal files it under "Mumbai Roadside Recipes"; Bombay Lives called it Bombay's new favourite snack). Hebbar's Kitchen's Manchurian gravy shows 4.99 from 308 votes and its dry cabbage Manchurian 5.0 from 47 votes; Veg Recipes of India's gravy recipe has at least 8 pages of reader comments; Sanjeev Kapoor, Tarla Dalal, Indian Healthy Recipes, Spice Up The Curry and Chef Sanjyot Keer all publish versions, plus many Jain and air-fryer versions. Points come off for soggy or oily balls (a frequent home-cook complaint), high sodium and refined flour, and critics who find it heavy on sauces.

storage: Store the fried balls and the gravy separately. Both keep 2 days in the fridge in closed boxes (cool within 1 hour). Freezing is not recommended: Veg Recipes of India notes the vegetable balls change texture after thawing (they turn spongy). Reheat the balls in an air fryer or oven at 180 °C for 4–5 min (or a dry pan, covered, turning) so they crisp again; reheat the gravy in a pan on low with 2–3 tbsp water until it just bubbles (cornflour gravy thickens and turns jelly-like in the fridge), then add the balls. Balls already soaked in gravy turn mushy and are best eaten the same day.
leftoverRemix: Manchurian fried rice bowl. Quarter the leftover balls. Heat 1 tsp oil on high, add the leftover gravy and boil it down for a minute until thick, add 1 cup cold cooked rice and the ball pieces, and toss for 2 minutes with a splash of vinegar, black pepper and fresh spring onion greens. The broken balls soak up the sauce and the rice turns into a one-pan "Manchurian rice" sold by Mumbai street stalls.
burnOff: about 4.1 km of running (290 ÷ 70 kcal/km, for a 70 kg adult), or about 5.8 km of brisk walking (about 70 min at 5 km/h, using about 50 kcal/km for walking) (est.). With 1 cup veg fried rice (about 590 kcal): about 8.4 km running or 11.8 km walking (est.).

navratri.reason: maida and cornflour are grains, plus onion, garlic, soy sauce and table salt, which the common vrat rule set excludes; a vrat-flour version would no longer be Manchurian.

ekadashi.reason: maida and cornflour (wheat and maize) are grains avoided on Ekadashi in the most common rule set.

jain.reason: carrot, onion, garlic, spring onion and ginger are root or bulb vegetables; use the cabbage-capsicum Jain Manchurian (Sanjeev Kapoor) with onion-garlic-free sauces.

ramadan.reason: vegetarian, so no halal-meat issue; it is salty (about 2.1 g salt equivalent) and fried, so it suits iftar better than sehri, where salt raises thirst during the fast.

jain.reason: skip carrot, onion, garlic, spring onion and fresh ginger (root/bulb vegetables), use cabbage and capsicum only, dry ginger powder, and onion-garlic-free sauces (see Jain variant).

vegan.reason: no dairy, ghee, honey or egg; the balls are bound with maida and cornflour, and the sauce is soy, chilli sauce, ketchup and vinegar (check that the chilli sauce has no fish sauce, which Indian bottled chilli sauces normally do not).

pescatarian.reason: vegetarian, no meat, so it fits a pescatarian diet.

sattvik.reason: skip onion, garlic and spring onion and use onion-garlic-free sauces (the Jain variant's sauce works; carrot can stay).

glutenFree.reason: maida (refined wheat flour) binds the balls and ordinary brewed soy sauce is made from soybeans and wheat; a gluten-free version needs rice flour and tamari (see Gluten-free variant). No hing is used in the main recipe.

dairyFree.reason: no milk, curd, butter, ghee or cream.

description: A vegetarian, vegan, dairy-free Indo-Chinese gravy of fried cabbage-carrot balls; not gluten-free (maida, soy sauce); Jain, gluten-free and air-fryer versions below.

variants.name: Jain Manchurian (cabbage-capsicum balls, no onion or garlic)
